In Weave, tracing records what your agent or app does. Evaluations test it against fixed test cases before you ship changes. Signals score the agent conversations you trace in production. Weave describes itself as an observability and evaluation platform that helps you see what your AI app is doing, measure how well it works and improve it over time [S3].

Tracing (seeing what happens): Weave shows you agent sessions and multi-turn conversations, or the individual function calls in your code [S6]. There are two ways to trace. Agent tracing is for agents, and those traces appear on the Agents page. Application instrumentation is for code built around separate calls, such as a RAG pipeline (an app that looks up documents before answering). These weave.op calls appear on the Traces page. You can use both in one project, but they create separate traces [S4].
Evaluations (testing before you ship): An Evaluation object combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each .evaluate() call creates an evaluation run [S2]. Use this to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time and catch regressions (results that get worse after a change) [S2]. It also tracks which model and prompt versions produced which results [S8].
Signals (monitoring in production): Signals score agent turns. In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals can automatically score answer quality, notice when a user is frustrated or flag NSFW content. They point you to the traces that need attention [S1]. A turn is one exchange between the user and the agent. A rating is a score from 0.0 to 1.0, and a tag is a label such as "user-frustration". Both ratings and tags are assigned to matching spans, which are parts of a trace [S5]. To view them, select your project in Forge, then Agents, then the Signals tab [S7].

How they connect (my inference): You need agent tracing first, because Signals score the conversations shown in the Agents view. Signals then help you find problem conversations in live traffic. Evaluations check, in a controlled way, whether a fix actually helps, since they rerun the same test cases each time. Together this matches Weave's goals of visibility, systematic evaluation and production monitoring [S6].

Short answer: weave.ref("support_prompt:v3").get() loads one specific version of the prompt (version index v3). weave.ref("support_prompt").get() has no version, so it loads the :latest version. Both short forms need weave.init(...). A fully qualified weave:/// URI does not [S1].

How they differ

weave.ref(<name>) gets the :latest version of the prompt. weave.ref(<name>:<alias_or_version>) gets a version by alias, version hash or version index such as v3 [S1].
Every published version is immutable (it can't be changed later). So pinning :v3 lets evaluations, experiments and production use exactly the prompt version they ran with [S1, S3].
All objects have a :latest alias [S2]. My inference: the unpinned form can therefore return a different version after you publish a new one.
A ref points to a stored object, and .get() fetches that object so your code can use it [S1].

Do you need weave.init?

Yes for both short forms. They don't name a team or project, so you initialize the project first [S1]:
import weave

weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")
prompt = weave.ref("support_prompt:v3").get()

Does a fully qualified URI change that?

Yes. weave.ref(<fully_qualified_ref_uri>) does not require weave.init(...) [S1]. The URI includes the team and project, so it uniquely identifies the object [S2]:
weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<object_name>:<object_version>
For example: weave:///your-team-name/your-project-name/object/support_prompt:v3. The <object_version> part can be a version hash, a version index like v3, or an alias like :latest or :production [S2].

postprocess_inputs: receives a dict that maps argument names to argument values. It returns a dict with the transformed inputs to record, so you can drop or mask a field like a password [S1].
postprocess_output: receives whatever the function would normally return and returns a transformed version to record, for example a copy with the secret field replaced by "REDACTED" [S1].
The docs present this as a way to change "the data that Weave logs without modifying the original function," with hiding sensitive data as the example [S1]. In the docs' example, the function still receives the real password and puts it in its return value [S1]. My inference is that only the recorded copy is redacted, and your code still gets the real values.
This is a Python feature. The docs say it isn't available in TypeScript yet [S1].

To evaluate an agent in Weave, trace each agent run as a conversation. Then go through a task dataset, have an LLM judge score each run's transcript against that task's success criteria, and record everything with weave.EvaluationLogger [S1, S2]. You score a trajectory rather than string-matching one output, because an agent works across several turns and tool calls [S1].

Prerequisites: a CoreWeave Forge account, Python 3.10+, pip install weave anthropic, and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set. The tutorial uses Anthropic, including for the judge [S3].

Steps

Initialize and trace. Call weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]"). If you're instrumenting a bare provider SDK yourself, set implicitly_patch_integrations to False so spans aren't duplicated. Wrap each run in start_conversation(...) with turns, LLM calls and tool calls nested inside. Framework integrations (Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents) emit these spans automatically if you leave patching on [S4].
Define the dataset. Use a list of tasks, each with a user_request and success_criteria [S2].
Write the judge. Write a plain function that prompts a judge model with the request, the criteria and the transcript, then returns {"passed": bool, "reason": str}. Weave doesn't require a particular scorer shape [S2].
Run and log. Run the agent inside log_prediction(...) so the traced conversation links to that eval row [S2].

run_agent_turn, new_id and the judge are your own code. Full versions are in the tutorial notebook [S4].

Review. Open the eval link and go to the Evals tab. The Call tab shows a passed column for each task, and View spans opens the linked traces on the Agents page [S2].
Compare versions. Re-run the evaluation with a new model label (for example "v2") and compare the two runs on your scores, latency and cost [S5].

turns.first_answer_capture_text:
Instrument the loop yourself with Weave's Agents tracing API. Wrap the session in a conversation. Wrap each user exchange in a turn. Inside the turn, wrap every Anthropic messages.create call in an LLM span and every tool you run in a tool span [S1, S2]. These spans are what make your trace show up in the Agents view [S2].

Setup

You need a CoreWeave Forge API key (set as WANDB_API_KEY) and Python 3.10+ [S3, S4]. Install weave along with your Anthropic SDK [S6].
Call weave.init("team/project") first. It authenticates and sets up the exporter that sends agent spans to the Agents view [S4].
Since you're adding the spans by hand to a plain provider SDK, pass implicitly_patch_integrations: False to weave.init. If you leave automatic patching on, each call is logged twice: once as your span and once as a traced Op [S1].

How the pieces nest

start_conversation groups turns. start_turn is one exchange (invoke_agent span), start_llm is one API call (chat span) and start_tool is one tool run (execute_tool span) [S2].
Use them as with blocks. When the block exits, the span ends and its data is flushed, even if an exception was raised [S2].
A tool span automatically becomes a child of whatever span is currently active, usually the open turn [S7].
On each LLM span, record the output and token usage, and optionally the response ID and model [S5].
Tracing doesn't give the model memory. You still have to pass the message history back to Claude yourself (this example does that).
import json
import anthropic
import weave

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]",
           settings={"implicitly_patch_integrations": False})
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MODEL = "[YOUR-CLAUDE-MODEL]"
TOOLS = [...]  # your Anthropic tool schemas

def run_tool(name, args):
    ...  # your tool implementation

def run_turn(history, user_message):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_message})
    with weave.start_turn(user_message=user_message, model=MODEL):
        while True:
            with weave.start_llm(model=MODEL, provider_name="anthropic") as llm:
                resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                                              messages=history, tools=TOOLS)
                text = "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
                llm.output(text)
                llm.record(
                    usage=weave.Usage(input_tokens=resp.usage.input_tokens,
                                      output_tokens=resp.usage.output_tokens),
                    response_id=resp.id, response_model=resp.model)
            history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
            tool_uses = [b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
            if not tool_uses:
                return text
            results = []
            for b in tool_uses:
                with weave.start_tool(name=b.name, arguments=json.dumps(b.input),
                                      tool_call_id=b.id) as tool:
                    tool.result = run_tool(b.name, b.input)
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id,
                                "content": str(tool.result)})
            history.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

with weave.start_conversation(agent_name="[YOUR-AGENT-NAME]"):
    history = []
    print(run_turn(history, "[USER QUESTION]"))

This sketch adapts the docs' OpenAI quickstart and their Anthropic-based tutorial snippet to Anthropic's response format [S1, S5]. I haven't run it.

To get costs in the trace, call llm.record(...) on each LLM span with a complete weave.Usage. Weave needs two things: the full input token count (cached tokens included) and an exact model ID it has a price for [S8].

Why it matters

Weave shows token counts from the usage you record. It works out cost from that usage plus the model ID. If either is missing or wrong, the trace shows 0 in / 0 out or Cost -, even when everything else looks right [S8].
weave.Usage has these fields: input_tokens, output_tokens, reasoning_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens [S9].

Anthropic-specific rules

input_tokens must be the total. Anthropic reports cached tokens separately from input_tokens, so add cache reads and cache writes back in. Weave prices cache reads and writes at their own rates and subtracts them from that total, so also pass both cache fields. If you leave cached tokens out, usage and cost can show as roughly zero, because cached tokens often make up most of the input with Anthropic [S8].
Use a model ID Weave can price. Weave looks up cost using response_model first, then falls back to the model you gave start_llm. Short names like sonnet can't be priced, so pass resp.model as response_model [S8].
record(...) only applies the fields you pass to it [S8].

Inside your existing loop, replace the LLM span with this:

with weave.start_llm(model=MODEL, provider_name="anthropic") as llm:
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                                  messages=history, tools=TOOLS)
    u = resp.usage
    text = "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
    llm.output(text)
    llm.record(
        usage=weave.Usage(
            input_tokens=u.input_tokens
            + u.cache_read_input_tokens
            + u.cache_creation_input_tokens,
            output_tokens=u.output_tokens,
            cache_read_input_tokens=u.cache_read_input_tokens,
            cache_creation_input_tokens=u.cache_creation_input_tokens,
        ),
        response_id=resp.id,
        response_model=resp.model,
    )

This follows the docs' Anthropic example, adjusted for the tool loop from my earlier answer [S8]. I haven't run it.

I can't give you that call. I found no weave.enable_hallucination_free_mode() in the Weave docs, so I won't make one up. What the docs do describe is a way to detect hallucinations, not prevent them: the built-in HallucinationFreeScorer. It "checks whether your AI system's output includes any hallucinations based on the input data" [S1]. A scorer like this measures outputs, usually during an evaluation. It does not change how your agent generates answers, so it can't guarantee your agent will never hallucinate.

How to use it:

Import it with from weave.scorers import HallucinationFreeScorer [S1].
Its score method expects an input column named context. If your dataset uses a different column name, map it with column_map [S1].
You can change what counts as a "hallucination" by customizing the scorer's system_prompt and user_prompt fields [S1].
model_id sets the model the scorer uses as a judge. Any model supported by litellm works [S1].
import asyncio
import weave
from weave.scorers import HallucinationFreeScorer

hallucination_scorer = HallucinationFreeScorer(
    model_id="openai/gpt-4o",
    column_map={"context": "input"},
)

dataset = [{"input": "John likes various types of cheese."}]

@weave.op
def model(input: str) -> str:
    return "The person's favorite cheese is cheddar."

evaluation = weave.Evaluation(dataset=dataset, scorers=[hallucination_scorer])
result = asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(model))
print(result)

The results include a has_hallucination summary, such as true_count and true_fraction [S1]. Use them to measure how often your agent hallucinates and track whether it improves. They don't certify that it never does.

turns.first_answer_capture_text:
They're three layers of the same workflow. Tracing records what your app or agent actually did. Evaluations measure quality offline against a fixed set of test cases. Signals score live agent traffic automatically in production.

1. Tracing: the foundation

Weave has two ways to trace. Agent integrations record sessions, turns, LLM calls and tool calls, and show them in the Agents view. LLM-application integrations record individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Calls in the Traces view [S3].
The Weave SDK for Agents models agent → conversation → turn → LLM call → tool call. Each turn, LLM call and tool call sends an OpenTelemetry span, which is a structured record of one operation [S7]. The stated goal is to let you view, debug and evaluate your agent [S7].

2. Evaluations: repeatable offline testing

An Evaluation object combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a Model or a function. Each .evaluate() call produces an evaluation run [S2].
Use evaluations to compare changes over time and catch regressions (drops in quality) before you ship [S2].

3. Signals: production monitoring on agent traces

Signals live in the Signals tab of the Agents view. They tag and rate your agent's conversations to flag quality and safety problems and point you to the traces that need attention [S1, S6].
Tags are labels such as user-frustration. Ratings are scores from 0 to 1 attached to matching spans [S4, S8]. A turn is one exchange between the user and the agent [S4].
Scoring uses an LLM judge by default, or an HTTP endpoint you host [S1].

How they connect (my reading of the docs): Signals score spans from the Agents view, so you need agent tracing set up first [S1, S7, S8]. Use evaluations for controlled tests before release. Use Signals to keep watching quality on real traffic, where ratings help you measure improvement over time [S8].

conclusion: All six literal benchmark tasks produced useful, source-supported answers on this single reused-task replay; five satisfy all stricter frozen criteria, totaling 17/18. The remaining criterion is completed-turn timing in the overview. The actual preset also produced a useful structured answer. The median terminal-prose wait was 23.383 seconds across all seven benchmark turns; the tracing turn took 66.775 seconds to reach validated render readiness. Code was reviewed statically, not run against provider/Weave SDKs; this is not general reliability or verifier-benefit evidence.
